chapters.title: Move connections beyond the die
chapters.text: Look down at the central die. The surrounding area is useful routing space, not empty waste. Redistribution layers relocate dense die connections across a wider region. Compare the die outline with routes extending beyond it, and distinguish the size of the silicon from the size of its package.

chapters.title: Silicon, mold and copper
chapters.text: Descend to the material boundaries: silicon dies, surrounding molding compound, dielectric layers and metal traces form one structure. Colors identify function, not a vendor recipe. The ordered layers create visual clarity; the engineering challenge is how different materials deform together.

chapters.title: RDL rearranges the roads
chapters.text: Follow a die contact to an external solder ball through planar traces and interlayer vias. RDL is constrained routing, not arbitrary drawing: width, spacing, return paths and insulation all matter. Identify where the route changes layer and where it moves the connection outward.

chapters.title: Die first or routing first
chapters.text: Compare two flows: place dies before building redistribution layers, or form RDL before attaching dies. Both are fan-out approaches, but yield risks enter at different stages. The final outline alone does not reveal the process. Ask when valuable dies enter the assembly and what has already been tested.

chapters.title: A 3D structure in thin layers
chapters.text: Open the thin package into separated layers. Dielectrics separate metal layers, while vias connect selected locations. Thickness is exaggerated for visibility and must not be read as manufacturing scale. Check whether adjacent routes should be connected or electrically isolated; that distinction is the purpose of the layer stack.

chapters.title: Follow the return path
chapters.text: The reference conductor beside a signal is important too. Current needs a complete loop; a disrupted return path affects high-speed behavior. Use the overhead view to inspect routing and the section to inspect reference continuity. Together, the two views explain the electrical order behind the geometry.

chapters.title: Warpage is functional
chapters.text: A slight conceptual bend highlights mismatched thermal expansion. Warpage can affect alignment, joining and board assembly; it is more than a cosmetic defect. The animated bend is exaggerated. Evaluation requires measurements, material properties and a mechanical model with explicit boundary conditions.

chapters.title: When alignment becomes a defect
chapters.text: Pause beside a contact and imagine the die shifting slightly. Would the intended route still land correctly? Inspection must address alignment, opens, shorts and interface defects. Each suspected issue needs traceable measurement; a visually touching animated connection is not evidence of a functional joint.

chapters.title: Thinness versus complexity
chapters.text: Step back: fan-out offers flexible connection placement and thin integration, while more layers, finer routing or larger area raise process demands. It is not automatically cheaper. Compare alternatives at equal function, test coverage and qualified output, rather than comparing package outlines alone.

chapters.title: Let connections guide the flow
chapters.text: Take this route with you: define connections and size, select die-first or RDL-first integration, plan routing, manage warpage and verify electrical behavior and reliability. Fan-out turns crowded die exits into an orderly network that must be manufacturable and inspectable, not merely visually elegant.
